sessions.title: Orthogonal is not orthonormal
sessions.focus: Distinguish orthogonal from orthonormal lists, normalize nonzero directions, and connect orthogonality to independence.
sessions.purpose: M13 introduced pairwise dot-product orthogonality; M15 needs list-level structure before coordinates and projection.
sessions.centralCapability: Classify and normalize fresh vector lists and prove the exact nonzero-hypothesis theorem linking orthogonality to independence.
sessions.principalObstacle: Orthogonal is confused with unit length, and the zero vector is allowed into an independence proof.
entryPrerequisites: M13 dot products, norms and orthogonality
requiredOwnership: Distinguish pairwise orthogonality from orthonormality and normalize a nonzero orthogonal list.
Prove that a finite pairwise-orthogonal list of nonzero vectors is linearly independent.
Diagnose the zero-vector boundary: pairwise zero dot products alone do not imply independence if the list contains 0.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a plausible theorem overextension caused by a hidden zero vector.
sessions.exitCondition: Correctly classify, normalize and prove independence for a fresh list while handling the zero-vector exception.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. M13 let us test whether two vectors are perpendicular by a dot product. M15 needs a coordinate-system version of that idea. A list is orthogonal when every distinct pair has dot product zero. It is orthonormal only when it is orthogonal and every member also has norm one. Those are different claims.

Define and connect. If u≠0, then q=u/||u|| has norm one and keeps the same direction. Normalizing each member of an orthogonal nonzero list preserves every zero cross-dot-product. The zero vector is special: it is orthogonal to everything, but cannot be normalized and makes any containing list dependent.

Explain. If c1u1+...+ckuk=0 for nonzero pairwise-orthogonal ui, dot with uj. All cross terms vanish and give cj||uj||^2=0. Since ||uj||^2>0, cj=0. Repeating for every j proves independence and shows exactly where nonzero is required.

Worked example. a=(2,0) and b=(0,-3) satisfy a·b=0, but their norms are 2 and 3, so they are orthogonal, not orthonormal. Normalizing yields (1,0) and (0,-1).

Guided practice. For u=(1,1), v=(1,-1), compute the dot product and norms, classify the pair, normalize it, and state the extra hypothesis needed for the independence theorem.

Fade. Fixed tasks use a three-vector R^3 list and a theorem-audit trap; no classifications are supplied.

Distinction check. Pairwise orthogonality is a relation among vectors; orthonormality adds unit norm; independence follows only when every vector in the orthogonal list is nonzero.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. u·v=0 and both norms are sqrt(2), so the pair is orthogonal but not orthonormal. Divide each by sqrt(2). The independence theorem requires every member to be nonzero.

sessions.title: Orthonormal coordinates make geometry auditable
sessions.focus: Derive dot-product coefficients in an orthonormal basis and the finite Pythagorean/Parseval identity.
sessions.purpose: Projection becomes transparent only after the learner sees why orthonormal coordinates separate without interference.
sessions.centralCapability: Recover orthonormal coordinates by dot products, reconstruct the vector, and verify squared-norm decomposition.
sessions.principalObstacle: The formula ci=v·qi is memorized or applied to a basis that is not orthonormal.
requiredOwnership: Derive the coefficient formula ci=v·qi for expansion in an orthonormal basis.
Use orthonormal coordinates to reconstruct vectors and verify the finite Pythagorean/Parseval identity.
Keep the orthonormal-basis hypothesis explicit rather than applying dot-product coefficients to arbitrary bases.
sessions.transferScope: Use an incomplete ON list and interpret the leftover component rather than pretending the coefficients are complete coordinates.
sessions.exitCondition: Derive and use ON coordinate coefficients while detecting an incomplete orthonormal list.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. In an arbitrary basis, M13 coordinates can require solving equations. Orthonormal directions behave like independent sensors: dotting with one direction ignores every other direction.

Define. If v=Σciqi in an orthonormal basis, dot with qj. Because qi·qj=0 for i≠j and qj·qj=1, v·qj=cj. This is a theorem with an orthonormal-basis hypothesis, not a generic coordinate recipe.

Connect. Expanding ||v||^2=v·v makes all cross terms vanish, so ||v||^2=Σci^2. Each orthogonal coordinate contributes independently to squared magnitude.

Worked example. With q1=(1/sqrt(2))(1,1,0), q2=(1/sqrt(2))(1,-1,0), q3=(0,0,1), v=(4,2,3), coefficients are 3sqrt(2),sqrt(2),3. Their squared sum 18+2+9=29 equals ||v||^2.

Guided practice. For r1=(1/sqrt(2))(1,0,1), r2=(0,1,0), r3=(1/sqrt(2))(1,0,-1), w=(3,2,1), compute coefficients, reconstruct w and verify the squared-norm identity.

Fade. Main uses a rational ON basis; Transfer intentionally supplies only two ON directions in R^3.

Distinction check. Orthonormality licenses dot-product coordinates. Merely being independent or spanning does not.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Coefficients are 2sqrt(2),2,sqrt(2); they reconstruct (3,2,1), and 8+4+2=14=||w||^2.

sessions.title: Orthogonal complements
sessions.focus: Define W^perp, prove it is a subspace, and reduce a universal orthogonality condition to finitely many spanning-vector tests.
sessions.purpose: Projection needs a precise space for residuals, not an informal perpendicular arrow.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute and justify W^perp from span or constraint descriptions while preserving ambient-space meaning.
sessions.principalObstacle: Testing one convenient vector is mistaken for testing the whole subspace, or W^perp is placed in another ambient space.
requiredOwnership: Define W^perp and prove it is a subspace of the same ambient R^n.
Reduce orthogonality to an entire finite span to dot-product constraints against a spanning set.
Compute a basis for a concrete orthogonal complement with correct ambient-space meaning.
sessions.transferScope: Reverse representation from coordinate constraints to a span before constructing the complement.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute W^perp from fresh data and justify why finite generator checks cover all of W.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A residual should be perpendicular to every model direction, not merely one convenient vector. For W⊆R^n define W^perp={x∈R^n:x·w=0 for every w∈W}; both spaces live in the same ambient R^n.

Define and prove. 0 belongs to W^perp. If x,y∈W^perp and a,b are real, then (ax+by)·w=a(x·w)+b(y·w)=0 for every w∈W, so W^perp is a subspace.

Connect. If W=span(w1,...,wk), checking x·wi=0 for every generator is enough: every w is Σciwi and bilinearity then forces x·w=0. This proof licenses the finite shortcut.

Worked example. For W=span{(1,0,0),(0,1,0)}, x=(a,b,c) lies in W^perp exactly when a=b=0, so W^perp=span{(0,0,1)}.

Guided practice. For L=span{(1,1,0)}, solve a+b=0 and parametrize L^perp with two independent spanning vectors.

Fade. Main couples two constraints; Transfer starts from a constrained-set description instead of a span.

Distinction check. The definition quantifies over all of W; the generator test is a proved finite method, not the definition itself.

sessions.title: Every vector splits into model part plus perpendicular part
sessions.focus: Construct and prove the unique orthogonal decomposition v=p+r with p∈W and r∈W^perp.
sessions.purpose: Projection should emerge as one component of a structural decomposition, not a memorized formula.
sessions.centralCapability: Construct and verify the W/W^perp split and prove uniqueness via W∩W^perp={0}.
sessions.principalObstacle: Any algebraic split is mistaken for an orthogonal decomposition, or uniqueness is asserted without an intersection argument.
requiredOwnership: Construct p∈W and r∈W^perp with v=p+r for concrete subspaces.
Prove W∩W^perp={0} and use it to establish uniqueness.
Distinguish an arbitrary vector split from an orthogonal decomposition by checking both memberships.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a supplied line decomposition and independently recover its coefficient.
sessions.exitCondition: Produce and justify the unique model-plus-perpendicular split for a fresh target.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Orthogonal complements let us split a target into what lies in W and what remains perpendicular to W. We seek v=p+r with p∈W and r∈W^perp.

Explain uniqueness first. If z∈W∩W^perp, then z is orthogonal to itself, so ||z||^2=0 and z=0. If p1+r1=p2+r2 are two valid splits, then p1-p2=r2-r1 lies in both spaces, hence is zero.

Connect existence. With an ON basis q1,...,qk of W, define p=Σ(v·qi)qi. The residual has zero dot product with each qi and therefore with W; so r=v-p lies in W^perp.

Worked example. For W=xy-plane and v=(2,-1,4), p=(2,-1,0), r=(0,0,4). The algebraic split (2,0,0)+(0,-1,4) is not orthogonal because the remainder is not perpendicular to every xy direction.

Guided practice. For W=span{(1,1)} and v=(3,1), set p=t(1,1), impose residual orthogonality, solve t and verify both memberships.

Fade. Main uses a two-generator subspace; Transfer audits a proposed R^3 line decomposition.

Distinction check. v=p+r alone is cheap; p∈W and r∈W^perp create the special decomposition and its uniqueness.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. (3-t,1-t)·(1,1)=4-2t=0 gives t=2, so p=(2,2), r=(1,-1). Uniqueness follows from W∩W^perp={0}.

sessions.title: Projection onto one direction
sessions.focus: Derive projection onto a nonzero line from the defining orthogonal-residual condition.
sessions.purpose: The line case isolates the projection coefficient so the formula is understood as a consequence, not a mnemonic.
sessions.centralCapability: Derive and use proj_span(a)(v)=((v·a)/(a·a))a for a≠0, verify the residual, and track generator scaling.
sessions.principalObstacle: The scalar coefficient is confused with the projected vector, or the formula is applied when a=0.
entryPrerequisites: M13 dot products and scalar multiples
requiredOwnership: Derive the line-projection coefficient from the condition (v-ta)·a=0 with a≠0.
Compute the projected vector and residual and verify residual orthogonality.
Explain why changing a nonzero generator of the same line changes the coefficient but not the projected vector.
sessions.transferScope: Represent one line with two differently scaled generators and reconcile different scalar coefficients.
sessions.exitCondition: Derive, compute and verify a fresh line projection without treating its scalar coefficient as the answer.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S04 gave a unique decomposition v=p+r with p in a subspace and r perpendicular. On a line L=span(a), every candidate p has the form ta. We can therefore solve the defining orthogonality condition directly.

Define and derive. Require (v-ta)·a=0. Expanding gives v·a-t(a·a)=0. If a≠0, then a·a=||a||^2>0, so t=(v·a)/(a·a) and p=((v·a)/(a·a))a. The nonzero hypothesis is what makes the denominator legal.

Connect. The scalar t is a coordinate relative to the chosen generator; p is the geometric vector. Replacing a by ca with c≠0 changes t to t/c but leaves ta unchanged. Projection belongs to the line, not to a preferred scaling of its generator.

Worked example. Let a=(1,1) and v=(3,0). Then t=3/2, p=(3/2,3/2), r=(3/2,-3/2), and r·a=0. The fraction is not a defect; it is the exact coefficient demanded by perpendicularity.

Guided practice. Let a=(1,2), v=(5,0). Derive t from the residual equation, compute p and r, then check r·a before opening feedback.

Fade. Main uses a 3D line with a nonunit generator; Transfer uses the same line described by two different generators and asks for reconciliation.

Distinction check. Projection coefficient, projected vector and residual are three different objects. The coefficient depends on the generator scale; the projected vector does not.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. t=(5)/(5)=1, so p=(1,2), r=(4,-2), and r·a=4-4=0.

sessions.title: Projection onto an orthonormal subspace
sessions.focus: Generalize line projection to a finite-dimensional subspace with an orthonormal basis.
sessions.purpose: Orthogonal coordinates now become an algorithm for extracting the complete model component without solving coupled equations.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute p=Σ(v·qi)qi for an ON basis of W and verify r=v-p lies in W^perp.
sessions.principalObstacle: The formula is applied to a nonorthonormal spanning set, or only one basis direction is checked.
requiredOwnership: Derive the ON-basis projection formula p=Σ(v·qi)qi from orthogonal decomposition.
Verify the residual is orthogonal to every basis vector and therefore to W.
Construct a suitable ON basis when a subspace is described geometrically rather than already given by ON vectors.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real subspaces with explicit or easily constructed ON bases.
sessions.transferScope: A plane is given by an equation rather than an ON list; learner must choose a basis before projecting.
sessions.exitCondition: Project onto a fresh finite subspace and verify both model membership and residual orthogonality.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A line needed one coefficient. If W has an orthonormal basis q1,...,qk, S02 already tells us how to measure each W-direction independently. Projection is the sum of those independent components.

Define and derive. Set p=Σ(v·qi)qi. Clearly p∈W. For each qj, (v-p)·qj=v·qj-Σ(v·qi)(qi·qj)=v·qj-v·qj=0. By S03, the residual is orthogonal to the whole span W. Thus p is exactly the W component in the unique S04 decomposition.

Connect. The simple coefficient formula depends on orthonormality. For a nonorthogonal basis, subtracting components independently double-counts shared directions. We postpone the general-column case until the transpose bridge and normal equations are derived.

Worked example. For W=span{e1,e3} and v=(2,5,-1), the ON basis e1,e3 gives p=(2,0,-1), r=(0,5,0). Both residual dot products vanish.

Guided practice. Let q1=(1/sqrt(2))(1,1,0), q2=(0,0,1), and v=(2,0,1). Compute the two coefficients, p and r, and verify both dot products before feedback.

Fade. Main changes all values; Transfer supplies the plane as x=y, so an ON basis must be constructed rather than copied.

Distinction check. An ON basis lets coefficients separate. “Basis” alone is not enough for p=Σ(v·qi)qi.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Coefficients are sqrt(2) and 1. Hence p=(1,1,1), r=(1,-1,0), and r·q1=r·q2=0.

sessions.title: Why projection is the unique nearest point
sessions.focus: Prove the nearest-point theorem using orthogonal decomposition and Pythagoras.
sessions.purpose: Projection is not merely a perpendicular decomposition; its residual orthogonality certifies global Euclidean optimality over the entire subspace.
sessions.centralCapability: Prove ||v-y||^2=||v-p||^2+||p-y||^2 for y∈W and use it to establish unique nearest-point optimality.
sessions.principalObstacle: A perpendicular residual is treated as a local picture with no optimization meaning, or uniqueness is skipped when equality occurs.
requiredOwnership: Derive the Pythagorean distance identity for a projection p and arbitrary y∈W.
Use the identity to prove p uniquely minimizes Euclidean distance from v over W.
Audit a rival candidate quantitatively without assuming a picture is to scale.
sessions.transferScope: A rival point is claimed to be closer on a line; learner must falsify it through the identity and exact distances.
sessions.exitCondition: Given a projection and rival point, prove and quantify why the projection is uniquely closest.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Projection gives v=p+r with p∈W and r⊥W. Why should p be the closest vector in W? The answer is not visual intuition but an exact distance identity.

Define and derive. For any y∈W, v-y=(v-p)+(p-y). The first term lies in W^perp; the second lies in W. They are orthogonal. Pythagoras gives ||v-y||^2=||v-p||^2+||p-y||^2.

Explain optimality. The second term is nonnegative, so no y∈W can beat p. Equality holds only when ||p-y||^2=0, meaning y=p. Thus the projection is the unique nearest point, globally over the whole subspace.

Worked example. Let W be the x-axis in R^2, v=(2,3), p=(2,0). For y=(5,0), ||v-y||^2=18, while ||v-p||^2+||p-y||^2=9+9=18. The extra in-subspace move can only add squared distance.

Guided practice. For W={z=0}, v=(1,2,3), p=(1,2,0), choose y=(0,0,0). Compute all three squared distances and verify the identity before feedback.

Fade. Main uses a new plane and rival point; Transfer begins with a disputed line candidate and requires exact refutation.

Distinction check. Residual orthogonality is the structural condition; nearest-point optimality is a theorem derived from it. We do not use one as an unexplained definition of the other.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. ||v-y||^2=14, ||v-p||^2=9, ||p-y||^2=5, so 14=9+5. Any different y in the plane adds the nonnegative ||p-y||^2 term.

sessions.title: Gram–Schmidt: remove what earlier directions already explain
sessions.focus: Derive the two-vector Gram–Schmidt step from projection and preserve span while creating orthogonality.
sessions.purpose: The learner needs to manufacture orthogonal coordinates from ordinary independent directions before multi-vector and least-squares work.
sessions.centralCapability: Given independent v1,v2, form u1=v1 and u2=v2-proj_span(u1)(v2), prove u2⊥u1 and preserve span, then normalize.
sessions.principalObstacle: Projection is subtracted with the wrong coefficient, or orthogonality is checked without proving the new pair spans the same subspace.
requiredOwnership: Derive the two-vector Gram–Schmidt update by subtracting the projection onto the first direction.
Verify orthogonality and prove span(v1,v2)=span(u1,u2).
Normalize the resulting nonzero orthogonal pair and diagnose a flawed subtraction.
sessions.transferScope: Debug an incorrect orthogonalization step rather than execute a clean recipe.
sessions.exitCondition: Orthogonalize a fresh independent pair, prove span preservation, normalize and detect a wrong projection subtraction.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Projection can remove the part of one vector already explained by another. Gram–Schmidt repeats that idea to clean a spanning list without changing the subspace it spans.

Define. For independent v1,v2, set u1=v1 and u2=v2-proj_span(u1)(v2). By construction u2·u1=0. Independence ensures u2≠0; otherwise v2 would already lie in span(v1).

Connect span preservation. u2 is built from v1,v2, so span(u1,u2)⊆span(v1,v2). Conversely v1=u1 and v2=u2+proj_span(u1)(v2), so v2 lies in span(u1,u2). The spans are equal. Normalizing u1,u2 then preserves the same span again.

Worked example. v1=(1,0), v2=(1,1). u1=(1,0); subtracting proj onto u1 gives u2=(0,1). The cleaned pair is already orthonormal and spans the same plane.

Guided practice. With v1=(1,1), v2=(2,0), compute the projection of v2 onto v1, subtract it, verify orthogonality, and express v2 back as u2 plus a multiple of u1.

Fade. Main uses R^3 with nontrivial fractions; Transfer is a debugging task where a plausible subtraction fails the dot-product check.

Distinction check. Gram–Schmidt changes basis vectors but preserves their cumulative span. It is not trying to preserve each original direction separately.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. proj_{v1}(v2)=((2)/(2))(1,1)=(1,1), so u2=(1,-1), orthogonal to u1. Also v2=u2+u1, proving both original vectors lie in the cleaned span.

sessions.title: Gram–Schmidt at full depth: span, dependence and order
sessions.focus: Extend Gram–Schmidt to multiple vectors, subtract every earlier orthogonal component, and interpret zero residuals and order dependence.
sessions.purpose: Three or more directions expose the structural content of the algorithm: prefix spans are preserved, dependence is detected, and output basis depends on input order.
sessions.centralCapability: Execute full multi-vector Gram–Schmidt, prove/check prefix span preservation, diagnose a zero residual as dependence, and explain order dependence.
sessions.principalObstacle: Only the immediately previous component is subtracted; a zero residual is treated as an arithmetic accident; or the ON output is assumed order-independent.
requiredOwnership: Construct each new Gram–Schmidt vector by subtracting projections onto all previously constructed orthogonal directions.
Verify prefix span preservation and normalize a nonzero multi-vector output to an ON basis.
Interpret a zero new residual as dependence and explain why reordering inputs may change the ON basis while preserving the final span.
sessions.applicationScope: Small ordered finite lists in R^n.
sessions.transferScope: A dependent input list is presented, and the learner must predict/interpret the zero residual and compare a reordered run.
sessions.exitCondition: Orthogonalize a fresh three-vector list, preserve the correct spans, and diagnose dependent/order-sensitive cases.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. With three vectors, subtracting only the most recent component is not enough: the new direction must be perpendicular to the entire span already built. Gram–Schmidt therefore removes every previously constructed orthogonal component.

Define. Set u1=v1. For k>1, define uk=vk-Σ_{j<k} proj_span(uj)(vk). Because the uj are pairwise orthogonal, dotting uk with any earlier ui cancels exactly the ith projection and all other projection terms vanish.

Connect span preservation. Each uk is made from v1,...,vk, so the cleaned prefix lies in the original prefix span. Conversely vk=uk+Σ projections onto earlier uj, and those uj lie in earlier original prefix spans. Induction gives span(v1,...,vk)=span(u1,...,uk) at every stage.

Dependence and order. If uk=0, then vk lies in the span of earlier inputs; the zero is a dependence certificate, not a nuisance to normalize. Reordering an independent list can change the ON vectors because each subtraction depends on what came earlier, but the final span is unchanged.

Worked example. v1=(1,0,0), v2=(1,1,0), v3=(1,1,1) clean successively to e1,e2,e3. This transparent case shows all previous components are removed at the third step.

Guided practice. Let v1=(1,1,0), v2=(1,-1,0), v3=(1,0,1). The first two are already orthogonal. Remove both of their components from v3 and verify the remaining direction is along e3.

Fade. Main uses a fully nonorthogonal three-vector list; Transfer uses an exactly dependent third vector and then changes the input order.

Distinction check. Gram–Schmidt preserves spans, not original vector identities. A different order can produce a different ON basis of the same subspace.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. The v3 projection onto v1 is (1/2)v1 and onto v2 is (1/2)v2; subtracting both leaves (0,0,1). Omitting either earlier direction leaves a nonzero dot product.

sessions.title: Transpose as the column-orthogonality bridge
sessions.focus: Introduce only the real matrix-transpose facts needed to compress many column dot products into A^T y.
sessions.purpose: M14 did not own transpose. M15 must repair this prerequisite gap before normal equations rather than silently assuming A^T notation.
sessions.centralCapability: Form A^T with correct dimensions, derive (A^T y)_j=a_j·y for A=[a1 ... an], and interpret Null(A^T) as vectors orthogonal to all columns.
sessions.principalObstacle: Transpose is treated as an inverse, rectangular shape is ignored, or A^T y=0 is read as y=0.
entryPrerequisites: M14 matrix shape and matrix-vector action
requiredOwnership: Define transpose entrywise and track its shape for rectangular real matrices.
Derive and use (A^T y)_j=a_j·y for the columns of A.
Interpret A^T y=0 as y orthogonal to every column, not as y=0.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real matrices only; transpose is used as a compact Euclidean dot-product bridge.
sessions.transferScope: Solve Null(A^T) for a rectangular matrix and reinterpret it as a column-space orthogonal complement.
sessions.exitCondition: Translate fluently between column-wise residual orthogonality and the matrix equation A^T y=0.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Least squares will need one compact statement saying a residual is perpendicular to every model column. M14 taught columns and matrix-vector action but did not own transpose, so we introduce exactly the missing bridge here.

Define. If A is m×n, A^T is n×m with (A^T)_{ij}=A_{ji}; rows become columns and columns become rows. Transpose is a re-indexing operation, not an inverse. A rectangular matrix can always be transposed even when no inverse exists.

Connect to dot products. Write A=[a1 ... an] with aj∈R^m and y∈R^m. Row j of A^T is aj^T, so component j of A^T y is aj·y. Therefore A^T y=0 exactly when y is orthogonal to every column, equivalently to their span.

Worked example. For A=[[1,0,2],[0,1,-1]] and y=(3,4), A^T=[[1,0],[0,1],[2,-1]] and A^T y=(3,4,2). Those entries are the three column dot products with y.

Guided practice. For C=[[1,2],[2,0],[0,1]] and y=(1,-1,2), first state the shape of C^T and C^T y, then compute both column dot products and confirm the matrix product matches them.

Fade. Main changes shape/data; Transfer asks for an entire null space and geometric interpretation rather than one product.

Distinction check. A^T y=0 says y is perpendicular to Col(A). It need not say y=0 when the columns do not span all of R^m.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. C is 3×2, so C^T is 2×3 and C^T y is in R^2. Column dots are (1,2,0)·(1,-1,2)=-1 and (2,0,1)·(1,-1,2)=4, so C^T y=(-1,4).

sessions.title: General-column projection and the normal equations
sessions.focus: Derive normal equations from residual orthogonality for full-column-rank A and justify invertibility of A^T A without future spectral machinery.
sessions.purpose: This is the bridge from geometric projection to the matrix equation used in exact least squares.
sessions.centralCapability: Derive A^T(b-Ac)=0, solve A^T A c=A^T b, prove A^T A invertible under full column rank, and verify the residual.
sessions.principalObstacle: Normal equations are memorized, or (A^T A)^{-1} is used without checking full column rank.
requiredOwnership: Derive the normal equations from residual orthogonality rather than quote them.
Solve an exact full-column-rank projection problem and verify A^T r=0.
Prove A^T A is invertible under full column rank using x^T A^T A x=||Ax||^2 and M14 null-space logic.
sessions.transferScope: Audit two proposed coefficient vectors by residual diagnostics instead of solving normal equations from scratch.
sessions.exitCondition: Derive and execute normal equations with a public rank hypothesis, and audit a proposed solution through A^T r.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. With an ON basis, projection coefficients separate. General independent model columns need coupled coefficients. Write A=[a1 ... an], candidate p=Ac, residual r=b-Ac. The defining condition remains geometric: r must be perpendicular to Col(A).

Define and connect. S10 says perpendicular to every column is exactly A^T r=0. Substituting r=b-Ac gives A^T(b-Ac)=0, hence A^T A c=A^T b. These are the normal equations: a consequence of residual orthogonality, not the definition of projection.

Why the inverse is legal when columns are independent. If A^T A x=0, multiply on the left by x^T: 0=x^T A^T A x=(Ax)^T(Ax)=||Ax||^2. Thus Ax=0. Full column rank means Null(A)={0}, so x=0. A^T A is square with trivial null space and therefore invertible by M14. No eigenvalue or PSD argument is needed.

Worked example. Let C=[[1,0],[1,1],[0,1]], d=(0,2,1). Then C^T C=[[2,1],[1,2]], C^T d=(2,3), giving c=(1/3,4/3). The fitted vector is (1/3,5/3,4/3), residual (-1/3,1/3,-1/3), and C^T r=0.

Guided practice. Use D=[[1,0],[0,1],[1,-1]], g=(1,2,0). Compute D^T D and D^T g, solve for c, then check D^T(g-Dc)=0. Before feedback, state exactly where full column rank is used.

Fade. Main uses a third matrix and asks for derivation plus invertibility proof. Transfer supplies competing coefficient reports and forbids a from-scratch normal-equation solve.

Distinction check. Normal equations can have solutions even when Ax=b is inconsistent. Residual orthogonality means best attainable geometry, not zero residual.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. D^T D=[[2,-1],[-1,2]], D^T g=(1,2), so c=(4/3,5/3). The residual is (-1/3,1/3,1/3) and D^T r=0. Full column rank is used to prove A^T A has trivial null space and hence is invertible.

sessions.title: Orthogonal projector matrices: symmetry plus idempotence
sessions.focus: Package full-rank projection as P=A(A^T A)^{-1}A^T and distinguish orthogonal projectors from merely idempotent maps.
sessions.purpose: A projection operator should have checkable algebraic structure before later factorization/eigen modules reuse it.
sessions.centralCapability: Derive the full-rank projector matrix, verify P^2=P and P^T=P, and use symmetry to distinguish orthogonal from oblique idempotent projection.
sessions.principalObstacle: Idempotence alone is assumed to imply orthogonal projection, or P is treated as a black-box formula.
requiredOwnership: Derive P=A(A^T A)^{-1}A^T from the normal-equation coefficient solution under full column rank.
Verify idempotence P^2=P and symmetry P^T=P for an orthogonal projector.
Discriminate an idempotent nonsymmetric map from an orthogonal projector by checking its residual against its range.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite real full-column-rank matrices and small square projector matrices.
sessions.transferScope: Audit an idempotent but nonsymmetric matrix through an explicit residual/range counterexample.
sessions.exitCondition: Derive and validate a small orthogonal projector and reject an idempotent impostor.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S11 solved projection one target at a time. When A has full column rank, c=(A^T A)^{-1}A^T b, so the fitted vector is p=A(A^T A)^{-1}A^T b. The matrix multiplying b is the orthogonal projector onto Col(A).

Define P=A(A^T A)^{-1}A^T. Idempotence means P^2=P: once a vector is already projected into the model subspace, projecting again changes nothing. Substituting the formula and cancelling A^T A in the middle proves this directly.

Symmetry. For real matrices, (XY)^T=Y^T X^T. Also A^T A is symmetric, and the inverse of an invertible symmetric matrix is symmetric because ((M^{-1})^T)=(M^T)^{-1}=M^{-1}. Therefore P^T=P. These are bounded transpose support facts, not an invitation to spectral theory.

Why both matter. Idempotence alone describes projections that may travel along slanted directions. Symmetry is what makes the residual perpendicular to the range: if y=Pz lies in Range(P), then (x-Px)·y=x^T Pz-x^T P^T Pz=0 when P^T=P and P^2=P.

Worked example. P=diag(1,0) is symmetric and idempotent; it keeps the x-component and residuals are vertical, perpendicular to its range.

Guided practice. For P=(1/2)[[1,1],[1,1]], verify P^2=P and P^T=P, apply it to (4,0), and check the residual is perpendicular to span(1,1).

Fade. Main derives a 3×3 projector from a rectangular A; Transfer gives an idempotent nonsymmetric impostor.

Distinction check. Every orthogonal projector is idempotent, but idempotence without symmetry is not enough.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. P(4,0)=(2,2), residual=(2,-2), and its dot product with (1,1) is 0. Direct multiplication gives P^2=P and symmetry is visible.

sessions.title: Least squares: the best attainable answer to an inconsistent system
sessions.focus: Formulate Euclidean least squares as projection onto Col(A), derive residual orthogonality, and prove global minimality.
sessions.purpose: The learner must understand what least squares does when Ax=b has no exact solution before seeing statistical regression later.
sessions.centralCapability: Recognize an inconsistent linear system as an approximation problem, minimize ||Ax-b||^2 through column-space projection, and interpret the nonzero residual.
sessions.principalObstacle: Least squares is believed to make Ax=b exact or normal equations are treated as unrelated algebra.
requiredOwnership: Formulate least squares as minimizing ||Ax-b||^2 over coefficient vectors and reinterpret it as nearest-point projection onto Col(A).
Solve an exact full-column-rank least-squares problem and verify A^T r=0 with a nonzero residual.
Use orthogonal decomposition to prove global minimality rather than infer it from a stationary equation alone.
sessions.applicationScope: Deterministic exact Euclidean fitting; no sampling or regression inference.
sessions.transferScope: Collapse a multi-equation scalar fitting problem into a one-dimensional column-space projection and interpret the residual.
sessions.exitCondition: Turn a fresh inconsistent system into a least-squares projection and explain exactly what is optimized and what remains unexplained.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. M14 classified some systems Ax=b as inconsistent: b lies outside Col(A). M15 does not pretend the contradiction disappears. Instead it asks for the attainable vector Ax closest to b in Euclidean distance.

Define. Least squares minimizes ||Ax-b||^2. Since every Ax lies in Col(A), this is exactly the nearest-point problem from S07 with W=Col(A). The fitted vector p=A x_hat is the orthogonal projection of b, and residual r=b-p lies in Col(A)^perp.

Connect. S10 turns residual orthogonality into A^T r=0, yielding the normal equations. S07 supplies global optimality: for any other x, b-Ax=(b-p)+(p-Ax) with orthogonal terms, so ||b-Ax||^2=||r||^2+||p-Ax||^2≥||r||^2.

Worked example. Fit one common scalar x to the inconsistent pair x≈1 and x≈3. Here A=(1,1)^T, b=(1,3), and the normal equation gives 2x=4, so x_hat=2. The fitted vector is (2,2), residual (-1,1), which is nonzero but sums to zero and is orthogonal to the column (1,1).

Guided practice. For A=[[1,0],[1,1],[1,2]] and b=(1,2,2), form A^T A and A^T b, solve, compute the residual, and check A^T r before feedback. Say why a nonzero residual is not a failure of least squares.

Fade. Main uses a different design matrix/target; Transfer removes matrix notation and describes three incompatible scalar requests.

Distinction check. Least squares minimizes residual norm; it does not assert every original equation is satisfied. Statistical claims about noise, uncertainty or prediction remain outside this deterministic geometry.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. The solution is (7/6,1/2). Fitted values are (7/6,5/3,13/6), residual (-1/6,1/3,-1/6), and A^T r=0. The residual is nonzero because b is outside the column space; least squares makes it smallest, not zero.

sessions.title: Rank-deficient least squares: one fit, many coefficients
sessions.focus: Separate existence/uniqueness of the projected fitted vector from nonuniqueness of coefficient representations when columns are dependent.
sessions.purpose: The learner must not infer that singular A^T A destroys the least-squares fitted vector or that a unique fit implies identifiable coefficients.
sessions.centralCapability: Solve a rank-deficient least-squares problem geometrically, describe all coefficient minimizers as one representative plus Null(A), and keep pseudoinverse/minimum-norm selection deferred.
sessions.principalObstacle: Failure of (A^T A)^{-1} is mistaken for nonexistence of a least-squares fit, or fitted-vector uniqueness is conflated with coefficient uniqueness.
entryPrerequisites: M14 null space and complete solution
requiredOwnership: Explain why the orthogonal projection onto Col(A) exists uniquely even when A has dependent columns.
Describe all least-squares coefficient minimizers as the coefficient solutions of Ax=p, differing by Null(A).
Diagnose invalid use of (A^T A)^{-1} in a rank-deficient problem without importing pseudoinverse machinery.
sessions.transferScope: Duplicate columns create infinitely many coefficient minimizers for one unique fitted vector.
sessions.exitCondition: Produce the unique best fit and the full family of coefficient minimizers while explaining why no ordinary inverse is legal.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S11's inverse formula needed full column rank. What if columns are dependent? The attainable set Col(A) is still a finite-dimensional subspace, so S07 still gives a unique closest fitted vector p. What may fail is uniqueness of the coefficients that represent p.

Define. Least-squares minimizers are exactly the solutions of Ax=p where p=proj_{Col(A)} b. If x0 is one solution, M14 says every solution is x0+z with z∈Null(A). Thus coefficient ambiguity is the same old null-space ambiguity, now inside a fitting problem.

Connect to normal equations. A^T A becomes singular when A has nontrivial null space, so writing (A^T A)^{-1} is illegal. Normal equations can still characterize minimizers, but M15 does not choose a special coefficient among them. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse and minimum-norm rule belong to M17.

Worked example. Let A=[[1,1],[0,0]] and b=(2,1). Col(A)=span(e1), so p=(2,0), residual=(0,1). Every coefficient pair with x1+x2=2 gives the same p; Null(A)=span{(1,-1)}. There is one fitted vector and infinitely many coefficients.

Guided practice. Let the columns be a and 2a with a=(1,1). For b=(3,0), first project b onto span(a), then write the scalar equation on coefficients that reproduces that p. Do not try to invert A^T A.

Fade. Main uses a 3×2 rank-one matrix; Transfer uses duplicate columns and asks for the entire coefficient family.

Distinction check. Projection uniqueness belongs to vectors in Col(A). Coefficient uniqueness requires injectivity of the map x↦Ax. Those are different objects and different theorems.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Projection of (3,0) onto span(1,1) is (3/2,3/2). If A=[a,2a], then Ax=(x1+2x2)a, so every pair satisfying x1+2x2=3/2 is a minimizer. No inverse of A^T A is needed or legal.

sessions.title: Deterministic line fitting from a data table
sessions.focus: Translate a small affine line-fitting table into a design matrix and interpret fitted values/residuals purely deterministically.
sessions.purpose: Least-squares geometry should transfer to a familiar quantitative representation without prematurely importing statistical regression assumptions.
sessions.centralCapability: Build the intercept/slope design matrix from tabular data, solve the exact least-squares line, and audit residual orthogonality to both model columns.
sessions.principalObstacle: The matrix is treated as supplied magic, intercept/slope roles are reversed, or deterministic fit is mistaken for statistical inference.
requiredOwnership: Translate a table (t_i,y_i) into the deterministic model y≈alpha+beta t with design columns 1 and t.
Solve the exact two-parameter least-squares fit and compute fitted values/residuals.
Interpret residual orthogonality to the intercept and t columns without claiming sampling, causality or inference.
sessions.transferScope: A different irregular t-grid requires rebuilding the design matrix and interpreting the two orthogonality equations.
sessions.exitCondition: Turn a fresh data table into a deterministic least-squares model and state exactly what the fit does and does not establish.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Least squares is geometry before it is statistics. A table of input values t_i and deterministic targets y_i can be fit by a line alpha+beta t simply by choosing a two-column subspace of possible fitted-value vectors.

Define. The design matrix has first column all ones and second column t: A_i=(1,t_i). The coefficient vector x=(alpha,beta) produces fitted values Ax. Residual orthogonality to the ones column means residuals sum to zero; orthogonality to the t column means their t-weighted sum is zero.

Connect. These are geometric consequences of projection, not assumptions about random noise. Without a sampling model, least squares alone does not provide standard errors, p-values, causality or predictive validity. Those belong to later statistical modules.

Worked example. For t=-1,0,1 and y=0,1,2, A=[(1,-1),(1,0),(1,1)] and the exact line is alpha=1,beta=1 with zero residual. This is an exact-fit special case, not the general least-squares situation.

Guided practice. For t=0,1,2 and y=2,2,5, build A, compute A^T A and A^T y, solve alpha,beta, then check the two residual orthogonality sums.

Fade. Main changes grid/targets and has nonzero residual; Transfer uses an irregular t-grid so no symmetry shortcut should be assumed.

Distinction check. A deterministic least-squares line summarizes this table under a chosen Euclidean criterion. It does not by itself certify a stochastic regression model.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. The solution is alpha=3/2,beta=3/2. Fitted values are (3/2,3,9/2), residuals (1/2,-1,1/2); they sum to 0 and their t-weighted sum is 0.

sessions.title: Synthesis: choose the geometry, not a memorized formula
sessions.focus: Integrate orthogonality, Gram–Schmidt, projection and least-squares reasoning while choosing a method from representation and rank information.
sessions.purpose: M15 should exit with method selection and cross-checking, not a collection of isolated formulas.
sessions.centralCapability: Given an unfamiliar subspace/model representation, choose a justified route, compute the best component/fit, cross-check with an alternative M15 representation, and reject an invalid shortcut.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner reaches for dot-product coefficients on nonorthogonal columns, or blindly inverts A^T A without first classifying the representation/rank.
requiredOwnership: Choose an M15 projection/least-squares route from the given representation and justify why its hypotheses hold.
Compute and cross-check a projection using both general-column residual conditions and an orthonormal basis constructed by Gram–Schmidt.
Audit a plausible wrong solver that uses dot-product coefficients on nonorthogonal columns.
sessions.applicationScope: Small exact finite models combining multiple M15 representations.
sessions.transferScope: Two solution reports compete; learner must use residual diagnostics and hypothesis checks rather than recompute blindly.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve a fresh mixed-representation projection problem, justify method choice and detect a wrong method from its violated hypothesis.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. M15 has several routes to the same geometry. If an ON basis is already available, dot-product coefficients are simplest. If independent nonorthogonal columns are given, normal equations express residual orthogonality. If a clean basis is useful, Gram–Schmidt can manufacture one. If columns are dependent, do not invert A^T A; separate the unique fitted vector from coefficient ambiguity.

Method contract. Before calculating, identify the representation and rank facts. Ask: Are these vectors orthonormal? Are the columns independent? Do I need one target or repeated targets? Which theorem's hypotheses are actually satisfied? A formula is only legal after this check.

Cross-check. Different legal routes must produce the same projected vector because S04/S07 give uniqueness. Thus Gram–Schmidt plus ON projection can audit a normal-equation result, and A^T r=0 can audit an ON-basis result without repeating every step.

Worked example. Suppose W has the ON basis {(1/sqrt(2))(1,1,0),(0,0,1)}. For one target, use direct dot products; building a normal equation would be legal but needlessly indirect. By contrast, two nonorthogonal independent columns invite either Gram–Schmidt first or a direct normal-equation solve.

Guided practice. For columns (1,0,0),(1,1,0) and target (0,2,1), first reject direct dot-product coefficients because the columns are not orthogonal. Choose either Gram–Schmidt or normal equations, compute only enough to predict that the residual must be parallel to e3, and state an independent check.

Fade. Main requires a complete solve plus a Gram–Schmidt cross-check. Transfer is an adversarial comparison between a naive dot-product report and a residual-orthogonality report.

Distinction check. M15 ownership is geometry and exact reasoning. Naming QR, using pseudoinverse, or making numerical-stability claims would cross future module boundaries even if those tools could solve the same problem.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. The column space is the xy-plane, so the projected vector must be (0,2,0) and residual (0,0,1). Direct dot products with the nonorthogonal raw columns are not coordinates. A^T r=0 is an independent check; Gram–Schmidt could also produce e1,e2.
